Hon dog efter att ha blivit skjuten på en idrottsanläggning och händelsen har lett till stor oro. – Det är klart att det känns väldigt, väldigt obehagligt, säger justitieminister Gunnar Strömmer (M). Många i området kände den 25-åriga kvinnan som sköts till döds i Älvsjö i södra Stockholm i fredags. Hon arbetade med unga inom kommunens ungdomsverksamhet och sköts på övervåningen av en idrottsanläggning. Samtidigt var hundratals ungdomar på plats i en närliggande idrottshall där det pågick både fotbollsmatch och innebandymatch. – Det är klart att man känner ett stort obehag, säger justitieminister Gunnar Strömmer (M). Han säger att det är särskilt allvarligt när den här typen av våldsdåd sker mitt i samhället där andra människor rör sig, speciellt där barn vistas och berörs. Ännu är motivet bakom skjutningen oklart och de två minderåriga som gripits misstänkta för mordet nekar till brott. Möjligt hämndmotiv Enligt uppgift till SVT ser polisen hämnd som ett möjligt motiv, då en nära anhörig till kvinnan funnits med på en så kallad ”dödslista” . – Exakt vad det här är, och hur vi ska förstå det, är lite för tidigt för mig att säga, men jag har stor förståelse för att många känner sig berörda, säger Strömmer och fortsätter: – Jag har förstått att det här var en väldigt uppskattad medarbetare i stadsdelen, att det är en person som många idrottsföreningar har en relation till. Det är klart att det här framförallt är en stor tragedi för den unga kvinna som skjutits ihjäl och hennes familj. Samhället måste kliva fram Det är inte ovanligt att våldsdåd mot anhöriga leder till hämndaktioner. Men enligt Gunnar Strömmer är för tidigt att säga om det här brottet riskerar att leda till en våldseskalering i närtid. – Vi får avvakta och se vad man kommer fram till. Arbetet för att få boende i området att känna sig trygga menar Strömmer nu handlar om närvaro och om samspelet mellan polisen och kommun, genom stadsdelsförvaltningen och civilsamhället. – Samhället tillsammans måste i ett sånt här läge kliva fram, säger Gunnar Strömmer. sources.summary: Fastigheter nära kritisk infrastruktur, osannolika affärsplaner och köpare med kopplingar till rysk elit. Finland har stoppat 68 fastighetsaffärer sedan 2022 med hänvisning till säkerhetsrisker. I Sverige hade köpen sannolikt genomförts.

Finland har stoppat 68 fastighetsaffärer sedan 2022 med hänvisning till säkerhetsrisker. I Sverige hade köpen sannolikt genomförts. SVT Nyheter har tidigare berättat att svenska myndigheter saknar en generell möjlighet att stoppa utländska fastighetsköp , med hänvisning till nationell säkerhet. Trots varningar från Säpo och nästan tio års utredning. Frågan har blivit aktuell i Sverige sedan Försvarsmakten velat ta över en fritidsfastighet nära en marinbas i Stockholms skärgård. I Finland ser det annorlunda ut. Landet har skärpt sina regler för fastighetsköp av utländska medborgare, utanför EU. ”Vi kommer inte tillåta affärer om det inte går att utesluta ett hot mot den nationella säkerheten”, säger försvarsminister Antti Häkkänen till Yle . Totalförbud för ryssar Fram till den 1 september i år har 68 fastighetsaffärer stoppats i Finland. Sedan juli 2025 råder dessutom i princip förbud för ryska och belarusiska medborgare att köpa fastigheter. Enligt Rickard Lindholm, sakkunnig på finska försvarsministeriet, handlar det om att förebygga säkerhetshot. Ryska staten kan tvinga medborgare utomlands att agera i Rysslands intresse. – Vi vill förhindra att det på lång sikt uppstår ett massivt fastighetsägarskap som skulle kunna användas i en eventuell konflikt. Stoppar inte rätt personer De finska lagarna fyller en viktig funktion enligt Kari Liuhto, professor i underrättelseforskning vid Finlands försvarshögskola. Misstänkta köp kan stoppas i ett tidigt skede. Att använda expropriering är både svårare och mer kostsamt, säger han. Men samtidigt anser han att lagarna fokuserar för mycket på medborgarskap. – I de flesta fall stoppar vi inte rätt personer, konstaterar Kari Liuhto. Enligt honom använder rysk underrättelsetjänst mellanhänder, eller andra metoder, om den vill komma över en strategiskt viktig fastighet. – De flesta ryska fastighetsköp i Finland har inget med underrättelseverksamhet att göra. Risken ökar Finska myndigheter är medvetna om risken för köp via bulvaner, och att den risken ökat sedan ett år tillbaka, när ryska köp stoppas helt. – Vi har möjligheter att ingripa mot misstänkta bulvaner, men utmaningen är att hitta dem, konstaterar Rickard Lindholm på finska försvarsministeriet. Trots luckor i lagstiftningen anser han att säkerhetshotande fastighetsköp ändå försvåras, eftersom köp granskas. – Den avskräckande effekten är det mest centrala. sources.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
sources.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
sources.text: Figure caption, Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos By Monica Garnsey BBC Eye Published 4 hours ago Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia. One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil. He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs. The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves. He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow , Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities. The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself." And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out. The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this. There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify. Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Two men tell of secret operations inside Russia. Watch on iPlayer Listen to the Podcast on BBC Sounds. If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube , external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome. "At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the warâ¦ Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says. His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets. "When these [drone] components are combinedâ¦ it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said. He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield. If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades. Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance. Image caption, Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers "You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers. Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information. He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets. "This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live. "In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points." He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints. Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals. "As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not." But he argued that his team's actions were justified. "I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared." Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves. Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule." But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance. Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event. Foma did his own digging on Ivan. After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year , external . One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians. Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too. "The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said. To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside. Foma has the same rule for his operatives. "As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said. Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work. "Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said. Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands. Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities. So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return. Image caption, Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travel Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him. "You go to a third countryâ¦ where [Ukraine's] agents meet youâ¦ and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him. Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school". But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress. Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag. "There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holesâ¦ and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon. Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where. Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work. "Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia." But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change. "Putin won't live forever," he said. Related topics War in Ukraine Russia Ukraine Spying Drones

sources.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
sources.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.
sources.text: Image source, Reuters By Jack Burgess Â and Â Toby Mann Published 18 October 2026 Updated 5 hours ago US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table". Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened. Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake". Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed. In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now". Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%. In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ukraine's President Zelensky attended an EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia. Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks. Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues. However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds. Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence. sources.title: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
sources.summary: Prosecutors say Paul Mackenzie lured the latest victims to their deaths by writing notes from his prison cell.
sources.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Paul Mackenzie operated his church for 16 years, attracting thousands of followers By Thomas Mukhwana Africa correspondent ,Â Reporting from Shakahola Published 1 hour ago A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie. Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 children. His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil". Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die. Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution. Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult are facing a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country. Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (Â£6) a day. "Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old." "We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets". Image source, Salim Karisa Image caption, Salim Karisa was paid about $8 a day to dig up dozens of bodies Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside." Stephen Mwiti, 48, recounted losing all six of his children to the cult and seeing "many bald women and tens of children" surrounding Mackenzie in his house when he went to confront him. Mackenzie forbade make-up and hairstyles, so told women to shave off their hair or keep it unkempt. Mwiti's former wife is one of those accused alongside Mackenzie. "If I met Pastor Mackenzie today, one of us will have to die," told the BBC. Image source, Mohamed Madi / BBC Image caption, Stephen Mwiti says his six children died in the forest "All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel." "This little thing here was the start of all my misery," Mwiti said as he pointed at a dusty TV and cable box in his home in the coastal town of Malindi, 70km (43 miles) from Shakahola. It was from that TV that Mackenzie's doctrine made it to his home. The pastor established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in the church's branches across Kenya. His church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi. His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil". Image caption, This is the building from where Mackenzie broadcast his sermons Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning." The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons". The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned. "My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said. The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said. By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers. Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover. "My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said. "I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest." Image caption, Peter Shukrani says he would have died if he had stayed in the forest but still believes Mackenzie is a good man In the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, all of the 191 victims Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children. Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery. Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said. "I still love him and he is still my pastor." In contrast Dan Mackenzie believes his father should be found guilty of murder. "He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing." sources.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
sources.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.
sources.text: Image source, Getty Images By Michael Race ,Â Business reporter Â and Â Simon Jack ,Â Business editor Published 5 hours ago The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in". He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market. A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy. The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations. It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels. There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey. Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures. "Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia. "Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help. "I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union." The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50â60%. The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years". "Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine. Image caption, Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on Ukraine Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer. But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment. All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently". At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added. Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began. Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids. "The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks." "Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged." Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history". "We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive." sources.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
sources.summary: At least one person was killed in the strikes, which also hit a data centre used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook.
sources.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The St Petersburg Oil Terminal was among targets hit in the city overnight By Aleks Phillips Published 18 October 2026 At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities. The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five. A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit. Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week. Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing. It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel. Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July . Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday. St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed. He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible. Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning. Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes". As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism , including from some US Republicans. However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps. Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year. Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years. Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter. Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said. sources.summary: Franske världstvåan Felix Lebrun blev för svår. Anton Källberg förlorade en tajt EM-final – efter att ha blivit utklassad i det avgörande skiljesetet. – Det kändes bra, förutom i de två sista seten då jag är i princip chanslös, säger en besviken silvermedaljör till SVT.

Anton Källberg förlorade en tajt EM-final – efter att ha blivit utklassad i det avgörande skiljesetet. – Det kändes bra, förutom i de två sista seten då jag är i princip chanslös, säger en besviken silvermedaljör till SVT. Tidigare under söndagen skrällvann Anton Källberg mot tyske världselvan Dang Qiu i semifinalen. Frågan var om den svenske 29-åringen skulle orka ladda om till finalen bara några timmar senare mot storfavoriten och världstvåan, fransmannen Felix Lebrun, 20. Svaret var ja. Källberg spelade fokuserat och tog hem det första setet med 11–7. Redan i andra set tvingande Källberg den unge fransmannen att förbruka sin timeout efter att ha tagit fyra raka bollar vid ställningen 10–5 till Lebrun. ”Timen” gav dock effekt och Lebrun skrek ut sin glädje efter setvinst med 11–9. ”Hur stark är han mentalt?!” Källberg, rankad 29:a i världen, spelade varierat och överraskade Lebrun flera gånger med långa servar. Trots att svensken spelade bra pingis vann Felix Lebrun det efterföljande setet med 13–11. Men Källberg reste sig återigen och kvitterade till 2–2 i set. – Hur stark är han mentalt?! frågar sig J-O Waldner retoriskt i SVT:s sändning. Finalen utvecklade sig till en förstaklassens nagelbitare. Källberg tog hem det femte setet med 11–9 och var bara ett set från ett historiskt EM-guld. Nära första svenska guldet på 26 år 2000 vann Peter Karlsson EM-guld i Bremen. Sedan dess har inte en svensk herrspelare vunnit EM i singel – och nu hade Källberg chansen att ta det första svenska EM-guldet på 26 år. Men, med kniven mot strupen gjorde Felix Lebrun sina två överlägset bästa set i matchen och vann de två avslutande seten med 11–6 och 11–1. ”Ska vara jättestolt” Anton Källberg åker från Slovenien med två EM-silver. I går förlorade han dubbelfinalen i par med Kristian Karlsson mot Felix och Alexis Lebrun. – På förhand hade man tagit två silvermedaljer, men just nu är det tråkigt. Det hade varit så fint med ett guld, säger Källberg. – Fantastiskt. Första singelfinalen och han står upp här och det har varit tuffa matcher hela vägen. Han har jobbat stenhårt från början av turneringen till nu. Han ska vara jättestolt över det han gör här, sammanfattar den svenska förbundskaptenen Michael Maze Anton Källbergs EM. Damernas final vanns av ryskan Elizabet Abraamian efter att hon besegrat tyskan Annett Kaufmann med 4–3 i set. Andra set höll på att utveckla sig i liknande riktning. Källberg hämtade ikapp en stor ledning för tysken. Och svensken löste finalbiljetten efter förkrossande 11–4 i det sjätte setet. – Han manglar honom! gastar J-O Waldner i sändningen. Jag kände att jag måste gå ut och visa att jag bryr mig, säger hon. Sabah Göranzon beskriver Kämpetorpshallarna som en plats där det brukar vara fullt med barn och ungdomar, liv och rörelse. Suzan Habib som bor i området beskriver den första känslan som oro och chock. – Jag börjar tänka på min egen tonåring som nyss gått på den skolan. Så det känns ju väldigt nära, säger hon när hon besöker platsen. – Det här önskar man ju inte någon ungdom. Det är supertråkigt att de ska behöva vara med om det här, säger Suzan Habib. ”Hammarby Fotboll i sorg” Många unga var på plats i lokalerna på fredagskvällen eftersom det pågick en innebandymatch och en fotbollsmatch arrangerad av Hammarbys Samhällsmatchen, som beskrivs som Hammarbys samhällsprojekt. ”Flera anställda inom Hammarby Fotboll har arbetat tillsammans med henne och känner henne väl, och det är med stor bestörtning vi tagit emot beskedet”, skriver föreningen på Instagram . Det är en fruktansvärd händelse och alla våra tankar går till familjen, anhöriga och medarbetarna i vår organisation, säger Lee Orberson, stadsdelsdirektör i Hägersten-Älvsjö. Enligt SVT:s utsända reporter har nya spänningar uppstått mellan demonstranter och polis i Paris under söndagen. I första arrondissementet i centrala Paris var det på söndag morgon omöjligt att hitta en enda orörd butik, rapporterar Le Parisien . Tobakshandlare, skönhetssalonger, apotek – alla hade krossade rutor, graffiti eller andra tecken på förstörelse. I hela landet uppges mellan 550 000 och 800 000 personer ha deltagit i lördagens protester , som började som en studentrörelse men vuxit till att involvera många olika grupper. Demonstrationerna har i stort varit fredliga men under lördagen urartade de i vad Le Figaro beskriver som ”urban gerillakrigsföring”. Även från städer som Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Montpellier och Nice rapporteras stor förstörelse. – Jag trodde aldrig att jag skulle se något liknande. De har förstört vårt arv, säger en invånare i Limoges, där stadshuset från 1800-talet brann, till Le Figaro. På söndag eftermiddag har nya spänningar uppstått mellan demonstranter och polis i Paris. Enligt SVT:s utsända reporter Tomas Thorén skringras maskerade demonstranter med tårgas på Place de la République. Borgmästarna i Paris, Marseille och Lyon skickade på lördag kväll ut ett gemensamt uttalande där man krävde ett möte med premiärminister Sébastien Lecornu nästa vecka, samt ”en tydlig och transparent utredning av den händelsekedja som ledde till denna situation”. Enligt henne tyder det på ”praktiskt taget ingen koppling” till studentrörelsen, säger hon till France Info.
